Week 5 Summary — Introduction to Linear Regression 

1. Statistical Learning Basics
	•	Goal: find relationships between predictors (X) and an outcome (Y).
	•	Two main objectives:
	•	Prediction — making accurate forecasts.
	•	Inference — understanding which variables matter and how.
	•	Methods:
	•	Parametric assumes a specific relationship form (e.g., linear regression).
	•	Non-parametric makes fewer assumptions but needs more data.

2. Linear Regression Concepts
	•	Assumes a linear relationship between variables.
	•	Uses Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) to estimate coefficients.
	•	Advantages: simple, interpretable, widely used.
	•	Limitations: assumes linearity, sensitive to outliers, depends on model assumptions.

3. Prediction vs Inference ￼
	•	Inference: focuses on explaining relationships and coefficient meaning.
	•	Prediction: focuses on accuracy and practical forecasting.
	•	A statistically strong model can still be ethically biased.

4. Model Evaluation
	•	In-sample fit uses R²; shows how much variation the model explains.
	•	Out-of-sample performance uses train/test split or cross-validation.
	•	Overfitting occurs when a model fits training data too closely but predicts poorly.
	•	RMSE and MAE measure prediction error.

5. Regression Assumptions
	•	Linearity: residuals should be random around zero.
	•	Constant variance: avoid heteroskedasticity (test with Breusch–Pagan).
	•	Normal residuals: important for inference, less for prediction.
	•	No multicollinearity: predictors shouldn’t be highly correlated (check VIF).
	•	No influential outliers: check leverage and Cook’s distance.

6. Improving Models
	•	Add meaningful predictors to improve fit.
	•	Use log transformations for curved relationships.
	•	Include categorical variables when appropriate.
	•	Balance model complexity with interpretability.

7. Key Ideas
	•	R² alone doesn’t prove a model is good; always test predictions.
	•	Diagnostic checks ensure assumptions hold.
	•	Visualization and interpretation are as important as computation.
	•	Ethical reflection matters in applying models to real data.
